parts.problem_md:
Compound **X** contains carbon, hydrogen and oxygen only. It has a relative molecular mass (*M*<sub>r</sub>) of 88.

The infra-red spectrum of **X** shows a strong absorption at 1745 cm<sup>−1</sup> but no absorption between 3200 cm<sup>−1</sup> and 3650 cm<sup>−1</sup>.

The proton (<sup>1</sup>H) NMR spectrum of **X** is shown in Fig 8.1

![Proton NMR spectrum with a quartet at 4.1 ppm, a singlet at 2.0 ppm, and a triplet at 1.3 ppm, displayed along a delta scale from 5 to 0 ppm.](assets/001-proton-nmr-spectrum-with-a-quartet-at-4-1-ppm-a-.png)

**Fig 8.1**

State the name of the compound used as a reference standard in proton (<sup>1</sup>H) NMR spectroscopy and state two reasons why it is chosen for this purpose.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The compound used as the reference standard in proton (<sup>1</sup>H) NMR spectroscopy is:
> 
> - Tetramethylsilane / TMS **[1 mark]**
> 
> Two reasons it is chosen are:
> 
> Any **two** from (1 mark for each point):
> 
> - It gives a single (sharp) peak because all 12 protons are in the same chemical environment
> - Its signal is far to the right / at 0 ppm / upfield (away from other signals)
> - It is chemically inert and does not react with the sample
> - It is volatile / has a low boiling point, so it is easy to remove after analysis
> 
> **[2 marks]**

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Compound **X** contains carbon, hydrogen and oxygen only. It has a relative molecular mass (*M*~r~) of 88.

The infra-red spectrum of **X** shows a strong absorption at 1745 cm^−1^ but no absorption between 3200 cm^−1^ and 3650 cm^−1^.

The proton (^1^H) NMR spectrum of **X** is shown in Fig 8.1

Proton NMR spectrum with a quartet at 4.1 ppm, a singlet at 2.0 ppm, and a triplet at 1.3 ppm, displayed along a delta scale from 5 to 0 ppm.

i) Using the IR data, identify the functional group present in **X**. Explain your answer.

[2]

ii) Use the proton (<sup>1</sup>H) NMR spectrum to deduce the structural formula of **X**.

Explain how you reached your conclusion by referring to the chemical shifts and splitting patterns of the peaks.

[4]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The functional group in **X** is:
> 
> - Ester / R−COO−R′ **[1 mark]**
> - Absorption at 1745 cm<sup>-1</sup> is characteristic of a C=O stretch of an ester (carboxyl C=O range: 1710–1750 cm<sup>-1</sup>); no O–H absorption (3200–3650 cm<sup>-1</sup>) confirms the absence of a carboxylic acid **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The structural formula of **X** is:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub>COOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (ethyl ethanoate) **[1 mark]**
> 
> Evidence from the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum:
> 
> - A triplet at δ 1.3 and a quartet at δ 4.1 indicate an ethyl group, –CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> **[1 mark]**
> - A singlet at δ 2.0 indicates a methyl group adjacent to a carbonyl, CH<sub>3</sub>–C=O (no neighbouring H atoms) **[1 mark]**
> - The signal at δ 4.1 indicates the CH<sub>2</sub> group is adjacent to an electronegative oxygen, –O–CH<sub>2</sub>– **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When using <sup>1</sup>H NMR data, start by matching splitting patterns before focusing on chemical shifts. A triplet and quartet pair is a strong indicator of an ethyl group.
> 
> Signals around δ 4 ppm usually suggest protons adjacent to an oxygen atom, while a singlet near δ 2 ppm often indicates a methyl group adjacent to a carbonyl group.
> 
> Only refer to IR evidence if it is explicitly provided in the question.

parts.problem_md:
A different compound, **Y**, contains a halogen atom. The mass spectrum of **Y** shows two molecular ion peaks, M<sup>+</sup> and [M+2]<sup>+</sup>, of approximately equal height (1:1 ratio).

i) State the identity of the halogen present in **Y**.

[1]

ii) Explain why the M<sup>+</sup> and [M+2]<sup>+</sup> peaks appear in this ratio.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The halogen present in **Y** is:
> 
> - Bromine / Br **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The M<sup>+</sup> and [M+2]<sup>+</sup> peaks appear in a 1:1 ratio because:
> 
> - Bromine exists as two isotopes, <sup>79</sup>Br and <sup>81</sup>Br **[1 mark]**
> - These isotopes have an approximately equal natural abundance (~50:50) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In mass spectrometry questions, recognise isotopic fingerprints:
> 
> - A **1:1 M**<sup>**+**</sup>** : [M+2]**<sup>**+**</sup>** peak ratio** indicates **bromine** (<sup>79</sup>Br : <sup>81</sup>Br ≈ 50:50)
> - A **3:1 M**<sup>**+**</sup>** : [M+2]**<sup>**+**</sup>** peak ratio** indicates **chlorine** (<sup>35</sup>Cl : <sup>37</sup>Cl ≈ 75:25)
> 
> If you see two peaks two mass units apart with equal height, bromine should be your first conclusion.

parts.problem_md:
Compound **P** is a naturally occurring chemical found in strawberries, apples and Parmesan cheese.

The percentage by mass is carbon 58.82%, hydrogen 9.80% and oxygen 31.38%.

The mass spectrum of compound **P** is recorded in Fig. 1.1.

![Mass spectrum of compound P](assets/002-mass-spectrum-of-compound-p.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

Calculate the molecular formula of compound **P**. Show your working.
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the molecular formula of compound **P**:

- Divide each percentage by the relative atomic mass to find the molar ratio:

C = $\frac{58.82}{12.0}$= 4.90

H = $\frac{9.80}{1.0}$= 9.80

O = $\frac{31.38}{16.0}$= 1.96

**[1 mark]**

- Divide by the smallest value (1.96) to find the empirical formula:

C = $\frac{4.90}{1.96}$= 2.5

H = $\frac{9.80}{1.96}$= 5

O = $\frac{1.96}{1.96}$= 1

C : H : O = 2.5 : 5 : 1

multiply by 2

empirical formula = C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>2</sub>

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate *M*<sub>r</sub> and confirm using the M<sup>+</sup> peak in Fig. 1.1:

*M*<sub>r</sub> of C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>2</sub> = (5 x 12.0) + (10 x 1.0) + (2 x 16.0)

*M*<sub>r</sub> of C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>2</sub> = 102

m/e = 102 peak

molecular formula = **C**<sub>**5**</sub>**H**<sub>**10**</sub>**O**<sub>**2**</sub>

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct calculations for C (4.90) **AND** H (9.80) **AND **O (1.96)
> 
> 1 mark for a correct empirical formula of C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>2</sub>
> 
> 1 mark for a identifying the m/e = 102 peak **AND **stating the correct molecular formula of C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>2</sub>

> **[exam-tip]**
> Use all available information: the percentage composition gives the empirical formula; the M<sup>+</sup> peak at m/e = 102 in the mass spectrum confirms the molecular formula.
> 
> Showing each step of your working helps identify errors and earns partial marks if the final answer is wrong.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Compound **P** is a naturally occurring chemical found in strawberries, apples and Parmesan cheese.

The percentage by mass is carbon 58.82%, hydrogen 9.80% and oxygen 31.38%.

molecular formula = C~5~H~10~O~2~

Table 1.1 shows the results of qualitative tests performed on compound **P**.

**Table 1.1**

| **Test** | **Observation** |
|---|---|
| **Addition of H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O** | Forms separate layers |
| **Na**<sub>**2**</sub>**CO**<sub>**3**</sub>** (aq)** | No visible change |
| **2,4-DNPH** | No visible change |
| **Tollens' reagent** | No visible change |

Deduce the functional groups present in compound **P**. Explain your answers with reference to Table 1.1.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> - **P** does not contain a carboxylic acid
> **AND**
> The Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> (aq) test is negative **[1 mark]**
> - **P** does not contain an aldehyde or ketone
> **AND**
> The 2,4-DNPH test is negative **[1 mark]**
> - **P** does not contain an aldehyde
> **AND**
> The Tollens' reagent test is negative **[1 mark]**
> - **P** could be an ester
> **OR**
> **P** could be an insoluble diol **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> It is often easier to state what functional groups are absent (from negative results) before deducing what is present.
> 
> Negative results are as informative as positive ones:
> 
> - Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> (aq) no change → no carboxylic acid
> - 2,4-DNPH no change → no carbonyl (aldehyde or ketone)
> - Tollens' no change → no aldehyde
> 
> An ester fits: it contains two oxygens, is insoluble in water and does not respond to any of these tests. A diol is also possible (higher alcohols are poorly soluble), but further evidence is needed to distinguish them.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Table 1.1 shows the results of qualitative tests performed on compound **P**.

**Table 1.1**

| **Test** | **Observation** |
| :---: | :---: |
| **Addition of H**~**2**~**O** | Forms separate layers |
| **Na**~**2**~**CO**~**3**~** (aq)** | No visible change |
| **2,4-DNPH** | No visible change |
| **Tollens' reagent** | No visible change |

Deduce the functional groups present in compound **P**. Explain your answers with reference to Table 1.1.

The carbon-13 (<sup>13</sup>C) NMR spectrum of compound **P** is shown in Fig. 1.2.

![Carbon-13 NMR spectrum of compound P](assets/003-carbon-13-nmr-spectrum-of-compound-p.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

Deduce the functional group present in compound **P**, using your answer to **(b)** and information from Fig. 1.2 and the Data Booklet. Explain your answer.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The functional group present in compound **P**:
> 
> - Ester **[1 mark]**
> 
> Explanation:
> 
> - The peak at δ = 162 ppm corresponds to the C=O of a carboxyl group (carboxyl range: 160–185 ppm) **[1 mark]**
> - The peak at δ = 63 ppm corresponds to a C–O group (C–O next to oxygen range: 50–70 ppm) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Match the observed δ values to the ranges in the Data Booklet:
> 
> - δ = 162 ppm falls in the carboxyl C=O range (160–185 ppm)
> - δ = 63 ppm falls in the C–O range (50–70 ppm)
> 
> An ester is consistent with both peaks, the presence of two oxygens in the molecular formula, and the negative results from parts (a) and (b). It contains a carboxyl C=O and a C–O–C linkage, neither of which reacts with Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>, 2,4-DNPH or Tollens' reagent.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Compound P is a naturally occurring chemical found in strawberries, apples and Parmesan cheese.

The percentage by mass is carbon 58.82%, hydrogen 9.80% and oxygen 31.38%.

Molecular formula = C5H10O2

Table 1.1 shows the results of qualitative tests performed on compound P.

Table 1.1
| Test | Observation |
| Addition of H2O | Forms separate layers |
| Na2CO3 (aq) | No visible change |
| 2,4-DNPH | No visible change |
| Tollens' reagent | No visible change |

P could be an ester or an insoluble diol.

The functional group present in compound P is an ester. The peak at δ = 162 ppm corresponds to the C=O of a carboxyl group (carboxyl range: 160–185 ppm). The peak at δ = 63 ppm corresponds to a C–O group (C–O next to oxygen range: 50–70 ppm).

The high-resolution proton (<sup>1</sup>H) NMR spectrum of compound **P** is shown in Fig. 1.3.

![High-resolution proton NMR spectrum of compound P](assets/004-high-resolution-proton-nmr-spectrum-of-compound-.png)

**Fig. 1.3**

Deduce the skeletal formula of compound **P**, using your answers to **(a)**, **(b)** and **(c)** and information from Fig. 1.3 and the Data Booklet. Explain your answer.
parts.solution_md:
The skeletal formula of compound **P** is:

![Skeletal formula of ethyl propanoate](assets/005-skeletal-formula-of-ethyl-propanoate.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct skeletal formula of compound **P**
> 
> Explanation:
> 
> Any **two** from (1 mark for each point):
> 
> - The spectrum shows two quartets and two triplets
> - A quartet arises from a –CH<sub>2</sub>– adjacent to a CH<sub>3</sub> (n = 3; n + 1 = 4 → quartet)
> **AND**
> A triplet arises from a –CH<sub>3</sub> adjacent to a CH<sub>2</sub> (n = 2; n + 1 = 3 → triplet)
> **AND**
> Each quartet/triplet pair identifies an ethyl (–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>) group
> - Two non-identical ethyl groups are consistent with the structure: one –O–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (ester oxygen side) and one –CO–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (acyl side)
> 
> **[2 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Several ester isomers share the molecular formula C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>2</sub>. The splitting patterns in the <sup>1</sup>H NMR identify the specific structure.
> 
> A quartet/triplet pair reveals an ethyl group. Two such pairs at different chemical shifts indicate two non-equivalent ethyl groups, which is the distinguishing feature of ethyl propanoate over other C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>2</sub> esters.

parts.solution_md:
The completed table is:

|---|---|---|

| **B** | 4 | 4 |

**[6 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for A having 3 peaks in the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum
> 
> 1 mark for A having 3 peaks in the <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectrum
> 
> 1 mark for B having 4 peaks in the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum

> **[exam-tip]**
> Count unique chemical environments, not the number of atoms. Use symmetry to spot equivalent atoms as they give a single peak.
> 
> For <sup>1</sup>H NMR, look for groups of protons in identical surroundings. For <sup>13</sup>C NMR, apply the same logic to carbon atoms.
> 
> In 2,2-dimethylpropane (**C**): all 12 H atoms are equivalent (1 peak in <sup>1</sup>H NMR), but there are 2 carbon environments, which are the central carbon and the four equivalent CH<sub>3</sub> carbons (2 peaks in <sup>13</sup>C NMR).

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Fig. 1.1 shows the skeletal formulae of three isomers of pentane, **A**, **B** and **C**.

In the high-resolution <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum of isomer **B**, the two methyl groups attached to carbon-2 give a doublet splitting pattern. The methyl groups in isomer **C** give a singlet splitting pattern.

Explain these splitting patterns in terms of neighbouring protons.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> - The splitting pattern depends on the number of adjacent / neighbouring protons **[1 mark]**
> - The methyl groups attached to C-2 in isomer **B** are adjacent to one neighbouring proton / a –CH– group
> **AND**
> n + 1 = 1 + 1 = 2 (doublet) **[1 mark]**
> - The methyl groups in isomer **C** have no neighbouring protons / are adjacent to a carbon with no H atoms
> **AND**
> n + 1 = 0 + 1 = 1 (singlet) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The n + 1 rule: the number of peaks in a splitting pattern = n + 1, where n is the number of H atoms on adjacent carbon atoms.
> 
> In 2-methylbutane (**B**), the two CH<sub>3</sub> groups on C-2 are each adjacent to C-3, which has 1 H. So n = 1 and the splitting is a doublet (2 peaks).
> 
> In 2,2-dimethylpropane (**C**), all four CH<sub>3</sub> groups are attached to a central carbon with no H atoms. So n = 0 and the splitting is a singlet (1 peak).

| **D** | Ethane-1,2-diol | Spectrum **D** shows a broad absorption at 3200–3600 cm<sup>-1</sup>, characteristic of the O–H stretch in an alcohol |

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for Spectrum **C** correctly identified as ethanedioic acid **AND** correct explanation
> 
> 1 mark for Spectrum **D** correctly identified as ethane-1,2-diol **AND** correct explanation

> **[exam-tip]**
> Ethanedioic acid is a hydrated solid acid, so O–H absorptions from both the carboxylic acid groups and the water of crystallisation are present. This makes it harder to distinguish from ethane-1,2-diol on O–H alone.
> 
> The clearest distinguishing absorption is the C=O stretch at 1670–1740 cm<sup>-1</sup> in ethanedioic acid, which is absent in ethane-1,2-diol.

The proton (<sup>1</sup>H) NMR spectrum of ethane-1,2-diol is shown in Fig. 2.5.

Use the spectrum to deduce the two proton environments in ethane-1,2-diol. State the number of peaks, their integration ratio and identify each environment.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> - There are two peaks, indicating two unique <sup>1</sup>H / proton environments **[1 mark]**
> - The integration ratio of the peaks is 2:1 (CH<sub>2</sub> : OH) **[1 mark]**
> - The larger peak corresponds to the –CH<sub>2</sub>– groups (4H) and the smaller peak to the –OH groups (2H); this is consistent with the structure of ethane-1,2-diol **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> State the ratio of proton environments, not the absolute number of protons. It is incorrect to say ‘two protons in one environment and one in another’ as the integration ratio 4:2 simplifies to 2:1.

parts.problem_md: State the number of peaks and the splitting pattern in the proton (<sup>1</sup>H) NMR spectrum of ethanedioic acid.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> For the proton (<sup>1</sup>H) NMR spectrum of ethanedioic acid:
> 
> - One peak / signal **[1 mark]**
> - No splitting / singlet **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Ethanedioic acid (HOOC–COOH) is a highly symmetrical molecule. Both carboxylic acid protons are in identical environments and are the only protons in the molecule, so there is only one <sup>1</sup>H environment.
> 
> There are no adjacent C–H groups (the C–C bond connects two carboxyl carbons, which bear no H atoms), so no spin-spin coupling occurs and the peak is a singlet.

parts.problem_md:
Compound **X** contains 62.1% C, 10.3% H and 27.6% O by mass.

i) Show that the empirical formula of compound **X** is C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O.

[3]

ii) The *M*<sub>r</sub> of compound **X** is 58.0. Deduce the molecular formula of compound **X**. Explain your reasoning.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
i) Showing that the empirical formula of compound **X** is C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O:

- Divide the percentage by mass of each element by its *A*<sub>r</sub>:

carbon = $\frac{62.1}{12.0}$  = 5.175

hydrogen = $\frac{10.3}{1.0}$ = 10.3

oxygen = $\frac{27.6}{16.0}$ = 1.725

**[1 mark]**

- Divide each value by the smallest (1.725) to give the simplest whole-number ratio:

carbon = $\frac{5.175}{1.725}$  = 3

hydrogen = $\frac{10.3}{1.725}$ = 5.97

oxygen = $\frac{1.725}{1.725}$ = 1

carbon : hydrogen : oxygen = 3 : 5.97 : 1

**[1 mark]**

- So, the empirical formula is:

**Final answer:** **C**<sub>**3**</sub>**H**<sub>**6**</sub>**O**

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for dividing the percentage by mass by the atomic mass for carbon **AND** hydrogen **AND** oxygen
> 
> 1 mark for the carbon : hydrogen : oxygen ratio ≈ 3 : 5.97 : 1
> 
> 1 mark for the empirical formula C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The molecular formula of compound **X** is:
> 
> - C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O
> **AND**
> The empirical formula mass (3 x 12.0 + 6 x 1.0 + 16.0 = 58.0) is equal to the *M*<sub>r</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To find the empirical formula:
> 
> - Divide the % by mass of each element by its *A*<sub>r</sub>
> - → Divide all values by the smallest to give the simplest whole-number ratio
> - → Multiply through if necessary to reach whole numbers
> 
> To find the molecular formula: calculate the empirical formula mass and divide the *M*<sub>r</sub> by it to find the multiplier. Here the multiplier is 1, so the molecular formula equals the empirical formula.

parts.problem_md:
A sample of a different isomer of compound **X** is cyclopropanol, which was analysed by NMR spectroscopy.

i) State the number of peaks in the carbon-13 (<sup>13</sup>C) NMR spectrum of cyclopropanol.

[1]

ii) Cyclopropanol was dissolved in CDCl<sub>3</sub> and the proton (<sup>1</sup>H) NMR spectrum of this solution was recorded as shown in Fig. 2.1.

![Proton (1H) NMR spectrum of cyclopropanol dissolved in CDCl3](assets/015-proton-1h-nmr-spectrum-of-cyclopropanol-dissolve.png)

**Fig. 2.1**

State the identity of a substance that can be added to the solution to identify the peak due to the –OH proton. State how the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum will change.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The number of peaks in the <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectrum of cyclopropanol is:
> 
> - 2 / two **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The substance that can be added is:
> 
> - D<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**
> 
> The change to the spectrum:
> 
> - The peak due to the –OH proton will disappear **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part (i): cyclopropanol has a line of symmetry through the C–OH carbon, making the two CH<sub>2</sub> groups equivalent. This gives only 2 carbon environments: the C–OH carbon and the two equivalent CH<sub>2</sub> carbons.
> 
> For part (ii): adding D<sub>2</sub>O causes deuterium to exchange with the labile –OH proton. The replaced proton no longer appears in the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum, so the –OH peak disappears. This technique is used to confirm the presence of –OH peaks in <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra.

parts.problem_md:
Lidocaine is used as a local anaesthetic. The structure of lidocaine is shown in Fig. 3.1.

![Skeletal formula of lidocaine](assets/016-skeletal-formula-of-lidocaine.png)

**Fig. 3.1**

A sample of lidocaine was analysed by carbon-13 NMR spectroscopy.

Deduce the number of peaks in the carbon-13 NMR spectrum of lidocaine.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The number of peaks in the carbon-13 NMR spectrum of lidocaine:
> 
> - Nine / 9 **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Lidocaine contains two sets of equivalent carbons due to molecular symmetry: the two Ar–CH<sub>3</sub> groups on the ring are equivalent, and the two N–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> groups are equivalent (giving one environment for the CH<sub>2</sub> carbons and one for the CH<sub>3</sub> carbons).
> 
> The nine distinct carbon environments are:
> 
> 1. Amide C=O
> 2. N–CH<sub>2</sub>–CO (methylene between N and carbonyl)
> 3. Aromatic C-1 (bearing –NH–)
> 4. Aromatic C-2/C-6 (bearing –CH<sub>3</sub>; equivalent pair → one environment)
> 5. Aromatic C-3/C-5 (–CH–; equivalent pair → one environment)
> 6. Aromatic C-4 (–CH–)
> 7. Ar–CH<sub>3</sub> (ring methyls; equivalent pair → one environment)
> 8. N–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>3</sub> (ethyl CH<sub>2</sub>; equivalent pair → one environment)
> 9. N–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>3</sub> (ethyl CH<sub>3</sub>; equivalent pair → one environment)

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Lidocaine was dissolved in CDCl~3~ and the proton NMR spectrum of this solution was recorded as shown in Fig. 3.2.

Table 3.1

| **δ / ppm** | **environment** **of proton** | **number of **^1^**H atoms** **responsible for the peak** | **splitting pattern** |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **1.2** | terminal methyl groups next to CH~2~ | 6 | triplet |

Explain why the absorption at δ 1.2 ppm is a triplet.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The absorption at δ 1.2 ppm is a triplet because:
> 
> - There is a neighbouring / adjacent –CH<sub>2</sub>– group
> **OR**
> There are two protons on the adjacent carbon (n = 2), so n + 1 = 3 (triplet) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The two equivalent terminal –CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> groups each have their CH<sub>3</sub> adjacent to a –CH<sub>2</sub>– (n = 2 neighbouring protons). By the n + 1 rule, the splitting pattern is a triplet.
> 
> Do not confuse the –N–CH<sub>2</sub>–CO– methylene (singlet, δ 3.0) with the –N–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>3</sub> ethyl methylenes; they are different environments with different splitting patterns.

parts.problem_md:
A chemist prepares and analyses some esters.

The chemist prepares an ester by reacting propan-2-ol with ethanoic anhydride.

Using structural formulae, construct an equation for the reaction of propan-2-ol with ethanoic anhydride.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equation, using structural formulae:
> 
> - (CH<sub>3</sub>CO)<sub>2</sub>O + CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>3</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>COOCH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> + CH<sub>3</sub>COOH **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The reaction of an alcohol with an acid anhydride produces an ester and the corresponding carboxylic acid, not water. The most common mistake is writing water as the second product by analogy with esterification using a carboxylic acid.
> 
> Take care with the structural formulae: isopropyl ethanoate (CH<sub>3</sub>COOCH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>) and ethanoic acid (CH<sub>3</sub>COOH) must both be written correctly.

parts.problem_md:
A sample contains a mixture of two esters contaminated with an alkane and an alcohol.

The chemist attempts to separate the four organic compounds in the mixture using gas chromatography. The stationary phase in the gas chromatograph column is a liquid alkane.

i) Explain how a liquid stationary phase separates organic compounds in a mixture.

[1]

ii) Deduce the relative retention times of these four compounds using the alkane stationary phase. Explain your answer.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) A liquid stationary phase separates organic compounds by:
> 
> - Their relative solubility in the stationary phase **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Deducing relative retention times:
> 
> - Both esters have the same functional groups
> **AND**
> they will have similar retention times **[1 mark]**
> - The alcohol is not soluble in the non-polar alkane stationary phase leading to a short retention time
> **AND**
> the alkane contaminant is highly soluble in the alkane stationary phase leading to a long retention time **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Separation in GC depends on the relative solubility of compounds in the mobile and stationary phases.
> 
> - Non-polar compounds (e.g. alkanes) are strongly attracted to a non-polar (alkane) stationary phase → longer retention times
> - Polar compounds (e.g. alcohols) are weakly attracted to a non-polar stationary phase → shorter retention times
> - Esters are polar but less so than alcohols; the two esters have the same functional groups so similar solubility → similar retention times
> 
> Without further information you can only state that the two esters will have similar (not identical) retention times.

parts.problem_md:
An ester is isolated from a perfume and analysed.

The percentage by mass of the ester is: carbon 66.63%, hydrogen 11.18% and oxygen 22.19%.

The mass spectrum and proton (<sup>1</sup>H) NMR spectrum of the ester are shown in Fig. 2.1 and Fig. 2.2 respectively.

![Mass spectrum of ester isolated from perfume](assets/018-mass-spectrum-of-ester-isolated-from-perfume.png)

**Fig. 2.1**

![Proton NMR spectrum of ester isolated from perfume](assets/019-proton-nmr-spectrum-of-ester-isolated-from-perfu.png)

**Fig. 2.2**

i) Calculate the molecular formula of the ester. Show your working.

[3]

ii) Use Fig. 2.1, Fig. 2.2 and the Data Booklet to deduce the skeletal formula of the ester. Explain your reasoning.

[5]
parts.solution_md:
i) To calculate the molecular formula of the ester:

- Divide each percentage by the relative atomic mass to find the molar ratio:

C = $\frac{66.63}{12.0}$ = 5.55

H = $\frac{11.18}{1.0}$ = 11.18

O = $\frac{22.19}{16.0}$ = 1.39

**[1 mark]**

- Divide by the smallest value (1.39) to find the empirical formula:

C = $\frac{5.55}{1.39}$ = 4

H = $\frac{11.18}{1.39}$ = 8

O = $\frac{1.39}{1.39}$ = 1

- So, the empirical formula:

C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate *M*<sub>r</sub> of the empirical unit:

*M*<sub>r</sub> of C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O = (4 x 12.0) + (8 x 1.0) + 16.0

*M*<sub>r</sub> of C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O = 72.0

- Confirm using the M<sup>+</sup> peak in Fig. 2.1:

m/e = 144

144 = 72.0 x 2

molecular formula = **C**<sub>**8**</sub>**H**<sub>**16**</sub>**O**<sub>**2**</sub>

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct molar ratio of C (5.55) **AND** H (11.18) **AND** O (1.39)
> 
> 1 mark for the correct empirical formula of C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O
> 
> 1 mark for identifying the peak at m/e = 144 **AND** a correct molecular formula of C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>16</sub>O<sub>2</sub>

ii) To deduce the skeletal formula of the ester:

- δ 3.8 ppm: –O–CH<sub>2</sub>– (2H, quartet; adjacent CH<sub>3</sub> gives n = 3, n + 1 = 4)
- δ 2.2 ppm: –CH<sub>2</sub>–C=O (2H, singlet; adjacent quaternary carbon bears no H atoms)
- δ 1.3 ppm: –O–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>3</sub> (3H, triplet; adjacent CH<sub>2</sub> gives n = 2, n + 1 = 3)
- δ 0.9 ppm: (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C– (9H, singlet; integration of 9 confirms three equivalent methyl groups; adjacent quaternary carbon bears no H atoms, confirming tert-butyl group)

The skeletal formula of the ester is:

![Skeletal formula of ethyl 3,3-dimethylbutanoate](assets/020-skeletal-formula-of-ethyl-3-3-dimethylbutanoate.png)

**[5 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for identifying δ 3.8 ppm as –O–CH<sub>2</sub>–, with supporting explanation/information
> 
> 1 mark for identifying δ 2.2 ppm: –CH<sub>2</sub>–C=O, with supporting explanation/information
> 
> 1 mark for identifying δ 1.3 ppm: –O–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>3</sub>, with supporting explanation/information
> 
> 1 mark for identifying δ 0.9 ppm: (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C–, with supporting explanation/information
> 
> 1 mark for the correct skeletal formula of ethyl 3,3-dimethylbutanoate

> **[exam-tip]**
> Work through the problem systematically:
> 
> 1. Calculate the empirical formula from % composition
> 2. Confirm the molecular formula using the M<sup>+</sup> peak at m/e = 144
> 3. Use the NMR spectrum to identify structural fragments
> 
> For the NMR fragment identification:
> 
> The peaks at δ 3.8 (quartet, 2H) and δ 1.3 (triplet, 3H) together identify an –O–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> ethyl ester group (δ 3.2–4.0 ppm = alkyl next to electronegative atom; δ 0.9–1.7 ppm = alkyl).
> 
> The peak at δ 2.2 (singlet, 2H) identifies a –CH<sub>2</sub>– adjacent to both the ester carbonyl and a quaternary carbon (δ 2.2–3.0 ppm = alkyl next to C=O; singlet because the adjacent quaternary carbon bears no H atoms).
> 
> The peak at δ 0.9 (singlet, 9H) is the key diagnostic for the tert-butyl group. Nine equivalent protons with no adjacent H-bearing carbon means three identical CH<sub>3</sub> groups on a quaternary carbon, –C(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>.

parts.problem_md:
The proton (<sup>1</sup>H) NMR spectrum of methyl cinnamate, C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, recorded using CDCl<sub>3</sub> as a solvent is shown in Fig. 1.1.

![The proton (1H) NMR spectrum of methyl cinnamate, C10H10O2](assets/021-the-proton-1h-nmr-spectrum-of-methyl-cinnamate-c.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

i) Explain why CDCl<sub>3</sub> is used as the solvent instead of CHCl<sub>3</sub>.

[1]

ii) State the purpose of adding tetramethylsilane (TMS) to the sample.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) CDCl<sub>3</sub> is used as the solvent instead of CHCl<sub>3</sub> because:
> 
> - CDCl<sub>3</sub> contains no protons / <sup>1</sup>H atoms, so it produces no peak on the spectrum
> **OR**
> CHCl<sub>3</sub> contains protons / <sup>1</sup>H atoms, so it produces a peak on the spectrum **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The purpose of adding TMS:
> 
> - It acts as a reference / reference standard, defining δ = 0 on the chemical shift scale **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> CDCl<sub>3</sub> (deuterated chloroform) is used as an NMR solvent because deuterium (<sup>2</sup>H) resonates at a completely different radio frequency and does not appear in the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum.
> 
> TMS (tetramethylsilane, Si(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>) is added as the reference standard. All other chemical shifts are measured relative to its signal at δ = 0.

| amide | RCON**H**R | 5.0 – 12.0 |
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The proton environment giving rise to the peak at δ = 3.8 ppm is:
> 
> - The –CH<sub>3</sub> group of the –OCH<sub>3</sub> / methyl ester group **[1 mark]**
> - It is a singlet because there are no adjacent / neighbouring protons **[1 mark]**
> - A peak area / integration of 3 indicates there are 3 protons in this environment **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Use three pieces of evidence to identify a peak:
> 
> 1. Chemical shift: δ = 3.8 ppm falls in the range for alkyl groups next to an electronegative atom (3.2–4.0 ppm)
> 2. Splitting pattern: a singlet means no adjacent protons (n + 1 = 1, so n = 0)
> 3. Integration: a value of 3 indicates 3 equivalent protons, consistent with a –CH<sub>3</sub> group
> 
> Only the –OCH<sub>3</sub> group satisfies all three criteria.

The skeletal formulae of the two ester isomers of C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>2</sub> that each produce exactly two singlets in their <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra are:

![Skeletal formula of methyl 2,2-dimethylpropanoate](assets/024-skeletal-formula-of-methyl-2-2-dimethylpropanoat.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct structure of methyl 2,2-dimethylpropanoate
> 
> 1 mark for the correct structure of tert-butyl ethanoate

> **[exam-tip]**
> Two singlet peaks with a 3:1 area ratio means two groups of protons in the ratio 3:1 (or 9:3, etc.) where each group has no adjacent protons.
> 
> An ester with –COOC– in the middle can carry a –C(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub> group on one side (9 H, singlet) and –OCH<sub>3</sub> on the other (3 H, singlet), giving a 9:3 = 3:1 ratio. Swapping the groups gives the second isomer.

parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The simplest whole-number ratio of protons in each environment:
> 
> - 2 : 2 : 2 : 3 : 3 **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) For the peaks at δ = 3.5 and δ = 1.2:
> 
> - δ 3.5 corresponds to a –CH<sub>2</sub>– group adjacent to an oxygen atom / –O–CH<sub>2</sub>– **[1 mark]**
> - δ 3.5 is a quartet because there is an adjacent CH<sub>3</sub> group (n = 3, so n + 1 = 4) **[1 mark]**
> - δ 1.2 corresponds to an alkyl –CH<sub>3</sub> group **[1 mark]**
> - δ 1.2 is a triplet because there is an adjacent –CH<sub>2</sub>– group (n = 2, so n + 1 = 3) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Integration values give the ratio of protons in each environment. The values 0.6, 0.6, 0.6, 0.9, 0.9 simplify to 2 : 2 : 2 : 3 : 3.
> 
> When explaining a splitting pattern, state three things:
> 
> 1. Identify the proton environment from the chemical shift and Table 1.1
> 2. Name the splitting pattern (singlet, doublet, triplet, quartet)
> 3. Justify using the n + 1 rule: state how many protons are on the adjacent carbon

Use Table 1.3 to deduce which of the four isomers **A**, **B**, **C** or **D** produced the <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectrum shown in Fig. 1.5.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> - **B** **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The spectrum shows four peaks, corresponding to four different carbon environments. Isomer **B** has exactly four:
> 
> - 30 ppm: three equivalent CH<sub>3</sub> groups of the *tert*-butyl group (C–C=O range)
> - Just above 30 ppm: the central quaternary carbon of the *tert*-butyl group (C–O<sub>2</sub>R range)
> - 50 ppm: the –OCH<sub>3</sub> carbon (C–O range)
> - approximately 180 ppm: the ester C=O carbon (RC**O**OR, carboxyl range)
> 
> Count the peaks before assigning environments; this tells you which isomer to focus on.
